title: Ageism, Education, Delegation & Research
description: Ageism and its effects on health, issues in gerontologic nursing education and deprescribing, what today's older consumers want, the Five Rights of Delegation, and gerontologic nursing research.
keyPoints: Ageism (WHO, 2021): stereotypes (how we think), prejudice (how we feel), and discrimination (how we act) toward others or oneself based on age.
The primary issue in gerontologic nursing education is not whether to include gerontologic content but the extent of its inclusion.
Box 1.2 care models: PACE, NICHE, Guided Care, Culture Change, Transitional Care.
Older adults take 2–9 medications daily; up to 62.5% may be inappropriate. Deprescribing facilitators: education/training, CE in medication optimization, multidisciplinary collaboration.
Five Rights of Delegation (Box 1.4): Right Task, Circumstance, Person, Directions & Communication, Supervision & Evaluation.
If the client becomes unstable, the nurse reassesses (Right Circumstance). A UAP cannot modify a delegated task without consulting the nurse (Right Directions & Communication).
Federal research funding: NIA, HRSA, grants.gov, John A. Hartford Foundation. Smaller sources: Sigma Theta Tau, ANF, GAPNA.

review.bigIdea: What stands in the way of good care for older adults (ageism, uneven education, unsafe delegation), and how do practice and research move care forward?
objectives: Explore ageism as it relates to the care of older adults in various settings.
Identify the issues influencing gerontologic nursing education.
Analyze the issues affecting gerontologic nursing research.

blocks.a:
"The stereotypes (how we think), prejudice (how we feel) and discrimination (how we act) towards others or oneself based on age."
Examples: birthday cards that mock aging, sitcom jokes about forgetful older characters, "senior moments."

blocks.q: How does ageism affect health, and what helps?
blocks.a:
Everyday ageism may be harmful to health and is linked to anxiety and depression.
Interventions that improve self-image and decrease negative self-talk and emotions reduce its effects.

blocks.q: What is the primary issue in gerontologic nursing education?
blocks.a:
"Not whether to include gerontologic nursing content but the extent of its inclusion."
Faculty with formal gerontologic preparation are imperative, and faculty must also counteract ageism.
Programs need clinical sites outside institutions.

blocks.title: Education documents by year
rows: NGNA Core Curriculum, 2nd ed. (Luggen & Meiner; NGNA now disbanded)
Core Competencies for Gerontological Nurse Educators (Box 1.3)

blocks.q: Box 1.2: which care models must students compare? What else stands out?
blocks.a:
Care models: PACE, NICHE, Guided Care, Culture Change, Transitional Care.
Also: use valid and reliable assessment tools; identify mistreatment and refer; manage geriatric syndromes; give restraint-free care (physical and chemical); ensure safe transitions; advocate for palliative and hospice care; prevent falls, medication mismanagement, and pressure injuries.

blocks.title: Box 1.3: The 7 gerontological nurse educator competencies

blocks.q: Evidence-based practice on deprescribing: numbers and facilitators?
blocks.a:
Older adults take 2–9 medications daily; up to 62.5% are inappropriate, harmful, or redundant.
Review of 24 studies (2005–2019). Facilitators:
1. Education and training in deprescribing
2. CE in medication optimization
3. Multidisciplinary collaboration
The nurse's role includes medication reviews and discussing medications with patients.

blocks.text: Summarize from memory: Explain ageism using the think / feel / act model, with one example for each.

blocks.q: What do today's older healthcare consumers want?
blocks.a:
They are more knowledgeable, have more financial resources, and are more tech-savvy.
They want timely care, communication and coordination, shared decision-making, community resources (for example, transportation), and discharge planning and follow-up.
Psychological, social, environmental, and economic needs get equal consideration with physical needs.

blocks.q: What can UAP do, and what guidelines govern delegation?
blocks.a:
UAP (also called NAP) tasks: vital signs, minor first aid, assisting with rehabilitation, assisting with ADLs.
The 2019 NCSBN and ANA National Guidelines for Nursing Delegation (Box 1.4).

blocks.title: Box 1.4: Five Rights of Delegation
items: Right Task: the task is in the job description or policy
Right Circumstance: the patient is stable; if that changes, the nurse reassesses
Right Person: the delegatee has the skills (shared responsibility of nurse, employer, and delegatee)
Right Directions and Communication: specific and two-way; the delegatee accepts and cannot modify the task without consulting the nurse
Right Supervision and Evaluation: the nurse monitors, evaluates outcomes, and ensures documentation

blocks.q: Research: since when, and who funds it?
blocks.a:
Gerontologic nursing research has grown since the early 1980s, has informed legislation, and is integral to the Future of Nursing.
Federal: NIA, HRSA, grants.gov, John A. Hartford Foundation.
Smaller: Sigma Theta Tau, ANF, GAPNA.

blocks.text: Patient becomes unstable → the nurse reassesses (Right Circumstance). The UAP cannot modify a task without consulting the nurse (Right Directions & Communication).
Clinical judgment (p. 16): How and why is care of older adults different today than in 1960?
Clinical judgment (p. 16): Is it safe to assume care of multiple older adults will be similar? How could treating them alike enhance or compromise care?
Clinical judgment (p. 16): When in a nursing program should older adult content be taught: early, later, or throughout? Support your position.

blocks.title: Chapter 1 key points (p. 16)
blocks.text: Gerontologic nursing roles were shaped by growth of the profession, more education, demographic changes, and changes in healthcare delivery. 65 is the reporting standard, but turning 65 doesn't make someone "old"; don't assume all older adults are alike. People 65+ are about 17% of the U.S., and the fastest growth is now, as Baby Boomers reach 65. About 11% live in long-term care, a share that rises sharply with age. Sex and race are significant indicators of poverty. Most older adults have at least one chronic condition. Ageism is prejudice against the old because they are old. Gerontologic content belongs in all programs. Research guides practice and quality of life.

questions.stem: Using the WHO (2021) definition of ageism, which component refers to how we feel about others or ourselves based on age?

options.text: Stereotypes
options.rationale: Stereotypes are how we think.

options.text: Prejudice
options.rationale: Correct. Prejudice is how we feel.

options.text: Discrimination
options.rationale: Discrimination is how we act.

options.text: Self-talk
options.rationale: Negative self-talk is a target of interventions, not one of the three components.

questions.explanation: The WHO (2021) defines ageism as the stereotypes (how we think), prejudice (how we feel), and discrimination (how we act) toward others or oneself based on age.

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing examples of ageism on a medical unit. Which example represents discrimination (how we act)?

options.text: A nurse believes that most older clients are forgetful
options.rationale: This is a belief, which is a stereotype (how we think).

options.text: A nurse feels annoyed when assigned several older clients
options.rationale: This is a feeling, which is prejudice (how we feel).

options.text: A nurse skips discharge teaching because the client is 88
options.rationale: Correct. Withholding care because of age is an action, which is discrimination (how we act).

options.text: A client calls her own memory lapse a "senior moment"
options.rationale: This is an everyday ageist stereotype directed at oneself, not an act of discrimination toward a client.

questions.explanation: Ageism has three parts: stereotypes (think), prejudice (feel), and discrimination (act). Withholding care because of age is discrimination. Ageism can be directed at others or at oneself.

questions.stem: A 77-year-old client tells the nurse, "I'm just a useless old man now. I can't do anything right anymore." Based on the chapter, which nursing approach is most helpful?

options.text: Agree that decline is expected at his age so he can accept it
options.rationale: Agreeing reinforces self-directed ageism, which is linked to anxiety and depression.

options.text: Change the subject so he does not dwell on his negative feelings
options.rationale: Avoiding the topic does nothing to reduce negative self-talk.

options.text: Tell him that everyone his age struggles with daily tasks sometimes
options.rationale: This repeats an age stereotype rather than countering it.

options.text: Help him name his strengths to build a more positive self-image
options.rationale: Correct. Interventions that improve self-image and decrease negative self-talk and emotions reduce the effects of ageism.

questions.explanation: Everyday ageism, including ageism toward oneself, may be harmful to health and is linked to anxiety and depression. Interventions that improve self-image and decrease negative self-talk and emotions reduce its effects.

questions.stem: According to the chapter, what is the primary issue in gerontologic nursing education today?

options.text: The extent to which gerontologic content is included
options.rationale: Correct. The issue is not whether to include gerontologic content but the extent of its inclusion.

options.text: Whether gerontologic content belongs in programs at all
options.rationale: The chapter says the question is no longer whether to include it.

options.text: Whether certification should replace the RN licensure exam
options.rationale: Certification is usually voluntary and does not replace licensure; this is not the issue named.

options.text: Whether students should only train in nursing homes
options.rationale: The chapter calls for clinical sites outside institutions.

questions.explanation: The primary issue is not whether to include gerontologic nursing content but the extent of its inclusion. Faculty with formal gerontologic preparation are imperative, and programs need clinical sites outside institutions.

questions.stem: A nursing program is strengthening its gerontologic content. Which needs does the chapter identify? Select all that apply.

options.text: Faculty with formal gerontologic preparation
options.rationale: Faculty with formal gerontologic preparation are described as imperative.

options.text: Faculty who counteract ageism
options.rationale: Faculty must also counteract ageism.

options.text: Clinical sites outside institutions
options.rationale: Programs need community clinical sites, not only institutional ones.

options.text: Limiting older adult content to one elective
options.rationale: The Key Points say gerontologic content belongs in all programs.

options.text: Placing all clinical time in nursing homes
options.rationale: The chapter calls for sites outside institutions.

questions.explanation: Gerontologic content belongs in all nursing programs. The chapter calls for faculty with formal gerontologic preparation, faculty who counteract ageism, and clinical sites outside institutions.

questions.stem: Which document, published in 2010, lists the recommended competencies (Box 1.2) for baccalaureate students caring for older adults?

options.text: NGNA Core Curriculum, 2nd edition
options.rationale: The NGNA Core Curriculum (Luggen & Meiner) was published in 2002.

options.text: AACN Essentials of Baccalaureate Education
options.rationale: The AACN Essentials date from 2008.

options.text: AACN/Hartford Recommended Baccalaureate Competencies
options.rationale: Correct. The AACN/Hartford (HIGN) Recommended Baccalaureate Competencies (2010) appear in Box 1.2.

options.text: Core Competencies for Gerontological Nurse Educators
options.rationale: Work on the educator competencies (Box 1.3) began in 2015 and took 2 years.

questions.explanation: Education documents: NGNA Core Curriculum 2nd ed. (2002), AACN Essentials (2008), AACN/Hartford Recommended Baccalaureate Competencies (2010, Box 1.2), and Core Competencies for Gerontological Nurse Educators (begun 2015, Box 1.3).

questions.stem: A nursing student is assigned to compare care models for older adults listed in the AACN/Hartford baccalaureate competencies (Box 1.2). Which models should the student include? Select all that apply.

options.text: PACE
options.rationale: PACE is one of the Box 1.2 care models.

options.text: NICHE
options.rationale: NICHE is one of the Box 1.2 care models.

options.text: Accountable care organizations
options.rationale: ACOs are an integrated system type, not a Box 1.2 care model.

options.text: Transitional Care
options.rationale: Transitional Care is one of the Box 1.2 care models.

options.text: Culture Change
options.rationale: Culture Change is one of the Box 1.2 care models.

options.text: Concierge practices
options.rationale: Concierge practices are an integrated system type, not a Box 1.2 care model.

questions.explanation: Box 1.2 asks students to compare five care models: PACE, NICHE, Guided Care, Culture Change, and Transitional Care. MCOs, PCMHs, ACOs, concierge practices, and pay-as-you-go clinics are integrated system types.

questions.stem: A 90-year-old client with dementia repeatedly tries to get out of bed at night. Which action by the nursing student best reflects the Box 1.2 competency of restraint-free care?

options.text: Request a sedative so the client stays in bed overnight
options.rationale: Using medication to control behavior is a chemical restraint.

options.text: Look for the cause and use care that avoids restraints
options.rationale: Correct. Box 1.2 calls for restraint-free care, avoiding both physical and chemical restraints.

options.text: Raise all four side rails and tie the call light down
options.rationale: This restricts movement and functions as a physical restraint.

options.text: Apply a vest restraint until the family arrives later
options.rationale: A vest restraint is a physical restraint.

questions.explanation: Box 1.2 competencies include restraint-free care (physical and chemical), managing geriatric syndromes, safe transitions, and preventing falls, medication mismanagement, and pressure injuries.

questions.stem: A nursing student notices bruises in different stages of healing on an 82-year-old client's arms, and the caregiver's explanation does not match the injuries. What should the student do, in line with Box 1.2 competencies?

options.text: Recognize possible mistreatment and report it so it is referred
options.rationale: Correct. Box 1.2 includes identifying mistreatment and referring.

options.text: Accept the caregiver's account to avoid upsetting the family
options.rationale: Ignoring signs of mistreatment fails the Box 1.2 competency.

options.text: Confront the caregiver alone and ask for an admission of abuse
options.rationale: Confrontation is not the competency; the student identifies and refers.

options.text: Wait for the bruises to fade and then reassess at the next visit
options.rationale: Delay leaves possible mistreatment unaddressed.

questions.explanation: The AACN/Hartford competencies (Box 1.2) include using valid and reliable assessment tools and identifying mistreatment and referring. Recognizing and referring possible mistreatment protects the client.

questions.stem: Which are among the seven Core Competencies for Gerontological Nurse Educators (Box 1.3)? Select all that apply.

options.text: Advocate and role model
options.rationale: Advocate and role model is competency 2.

options.text: Interprofessional learning (IPE)
options.rationale: Interprofessional learning is competency 4.

options.text: Prescriptive authority
options.rationale: Prescriptive authority belongs to the AGNP role, not the educator competencies.

options.text: Integrate aging in curricula
options.rationale: Integrating aging in curricula is competency 5.

options.text: Case management
options.rationale: Case management is an AGNP function, not an educator competency.

options.text: Scholarship and leadership
options.rationale: Scholarship and leadership is competency 7.

questions.explanation: The seven educator competencies are knowledge and skills, advocate and role model, innovative teaching, interprofessional learning (IPE), integrate aging in curricula, evaluate learning, and scholarship and leadership.

questions.stem: A nurse is presenting evidence on deprescribing. Which statement accurately reflects the chapter's data on medication use?

options.text: Older adults take 10 to 15 drugs daily, and about 14% are inappropriate
options.rationale: The chapter reports 2–9 medications daily; 14% is the share of APRNs with a DNP.

options.text: Older adults take 1 to 2 drugs daily, and few are ever inappropriate
options.rationale: This understates both the number of medications and the share that are inappropriate.

options.text: Older adults take 2 to 9 drugs daily, and all of them are clearly needed
options.rationale: Up to 62.5% may be inappropriate, harmful, or redundant.

options.text: Older adults take 2 to 9 drugs daily, and up to 62.5% are inappropriate
options.rationale: Correct. Older adults take 2–9 medications daily, and up to 62.5% may be inappropriate, harmful, or redundant.

questions.explanation: Older adults take 2–9 medications daily, and up to 62.5% may be inappropriate, harmful, or redundant. A review of 24 studies (2005–2019) identified facilitators of deprescribing.

questions.stem: A clinic wants to improve deprescribing for its older clients. Based on the evidence review in the chapter, which strategies are facilitators of deprescribing? Select all that apply.

options.text: Education and training in deprescribing
options.rationale: Education and training is facilitator 1.

options.text: Stopping every drug once a client turns 85
options.rationale: Blanket stopping by age is not a facilitator and ignores individual review.

options.text: Continuing education in medication optimization
options.rationale: CE in medication optimization is facilitator 2.

options.text: Multidisciplinary collaboration
options.rationale: Multidisciplinary collaboration is facilitator 3.

options.text: Letting clients stop drugs on their own
options.rationale: The nurse's role is medication review and discussion with clients, not unsupervised stopping.

questions.explanation: A review of 24 studies (2005–2019) found three facilitators of deprescribing: education and training in deprescribing, CE in medication optimization, and multidisciplinary collaboration.

questions.stem: A 78-year-old client with uncontrolled hypertension brings a bag of eight medication bottles to a clinic visit. Which nursing action reflects the nurse's role in deprescribing?

options.text: Tell the client to stop the medications that seem unnecessary
options.rationale: Stopping medications is not done by the nurse alone; deprescribing relies on review and collaboration.

options.text: Tell the client to keep taking all of them exactly as before
options.rationale: This misses the chance to identify inappropriate or redundant medications.

options.text: Review the medications and discuss each one with the client
options.rationale: Correct. The nurse's role includes medication reviews and discussing medications with patients.

options.text: Throw away the old bottles and order new ones from the pharmacy
options.rationale: Discarding medications without review is unsafe and is not part of the nurse's role.

questions.explanation: Up to 62.5% of older adults' medications may be inappropriate, harmful, or redundant. The nurse's role includes medication reviews and discussing medications with patients, supported by multidisciplinary collaboration.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old client who researched his condition online says, "I want to help decide my treatment, and I need a way to get to my follow-up visits." Which response best reflects what the chapter says today's older healthcare consumers want?

options.text: Share decision-making with him and link him to transportation resources
options.rationale: Correct. Today's consumers want shared decision-making, community resources such as transportation, and follow-up.

options.text: Tell him to rely on his provider's decision instead of online research
options.rationale: Today's consumers are more knowledgeable and want shared decision-making.

options.text: Address his physical needs first and his transportation needs later
options.rationale: Social, environmental, and economic needs get equal consideration with physical needs.

options.text: Give him printed instructions so that follow-up visits are unnecessary
options.rationale: Consumers want discharge planning and follow-up, not fewer contacts.

questions.explanation: Today's older consumers are more knowledgeable, have more financial resources, and are more tech-savvy. They want timely care, communication and coordination, shared decision-making, community resources such as transportation, and discharge planning and follow-up. Psychological, social, environmental, and economic needs get equal consideration with physical needs.

questions.stem: An RN on a long-term care unit is making assignments. Which task is appropriate to delegate to unlicensed assistive personnel (UAP)?

options.text: Assessing a resident who has new shortness of breath
options.rationale: A resident with a new problem is not stable, and assessment is not a UAP task.

options.text: Taking vital signs on a resident whose condition is stable
options.rationale: Correct. Vital signs on a stable resident fit the UAP task list and the Right Circumstance.

options.text: Deciding whether a resident needs a home care referral
options.rationale: Referral decisions require nursing clinical judgment.

options.text: Changing a resident's care plan after the resident fell last night
options.rationale: UAP cannot modify care without consulting the nurse, and planning is a nursing function.

questions.explanation: UAP (also called NAP) tasks include vital signs, minor first aid, assisting with rehabilitation, and assisting with ADLs. The task must be in the job description or policy (Right Task) and the client must be stable (Right Circumstance).

questions.stem: An RN delegates ambulation of an 84-year-old client to a UAP. Thirty minutes later the UAP reports that the client is now dizzy and short of breath. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Have the UAP keep walking the client but more slowly
options.rationale: The client is no longer stable, so the delegated task cannot simply continue.

options.text: Assign the task to a different UAP for the next walk
options.rationale: Changing the delegatee does not address the client's changed condition.

options.text: Document the report and recheck at the end of the shift
options.rationale: Documentation alone delays needed reassessment.

options.text: Reassess the client and whether delegation still fits
options.rationale: Correct. Under the Right Circumstance, if the client's condition changes, the nurse reassesses.

questions.explanation: Right Circumstance requires a stable client. If the client's condition changes, the nurse must reassess the client and whether delegation is still appropriate.

questions.stem: A nurse delegates assistance with ambulation to a UAP, directing the UAP to walk a client twice in the hallway. The UAP decides to walk the client outside to the parking lot without telling the nurse. Which right of delegation was violated?

options.text: Right Task in the job description
options.rationale: Assisting with ambulation is an appropriate UAP task.

options.text: Right Person with the needed skills
options.rationale: Nothing suggests the UAP lacks the skills for ambulation.

options.text: Right Directions and Communication
options.rationale: Correct. The delegatee accepts the task and cannot modify it without consulting the nurse.

options.text: Right Circumstance of a stable client
options.rationale: The client was stable; the problem is that the UAP changed the task.

questions.explanation: Right Directions and Communication requires specific, two-way communication. The delegatee accepts the task and cannot modify it without consulting the licensed nurse.

questions.stem: An RN in an assisted living facility is reviewing which tasks UAP may perform. Which tasks does the chapter list? Select all that apply.

options.text: Taking vital signs
options.rationale: Vital signs are a UAP task.

options.text: Minor first aid
options.rationale: Minor first aid is a UAP task.

options.text: Assisting with rehabilitation
options.rationale: Assisting with rehabilitation is a UAP task.

options.text: Writing the plan of care
options.rationale: Planning care is a nursing function, not a UAP task.

options.text: Assisting with ADLs
options.rationale: Assisting with ADLs is a UAP task.

options.text: Evaluating outcomes of care
options.rationale: Evaluating outcomes is the nurse's job under Right Supervision and Evaluation.

questions.explanation: UAP (also called NAP) may take vital signs, give minor first aid, assist with rehabilitation, and assist with ADLs. The nurse plans care and, under Right Supervision and Evaluation, monitors, evaluates outcomes, and ensures documentation.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes the Right Person in the 2019 NCSBN and ANA National Guidelines for Nursing Delegation?

options.text: The task is listed in the delegatee's job description or facility policy
options.rationale: This describes the Right Task.

options.text: The delegatee has the skills; nurse, employer, and delegatee share this
options.rationale: Correct. The Right Person means the delegatee has the skills, a shared responsibility of the nurse, employer, and delegatee.

options.text: The nurse monitors, evaluates outcomes, and ensures documentation
options.rationale: This describes the Right Supervision and Evaluation.

options.text: The client is stable, and the nurse reassesses if this changes
options.rationale: This describes the Right Circumstance.

questions.explanation: The Five Rights (Box 1.4): Right Task (in the job description or policy), Right Circumstance (client stable), Right Person (delegatee has the skills), Right Directions and Communication (specific, two-way), and Right Supervision and Evaluation (nurse monitors and evaluates).

questions.stem: A nurse researcher plans a study on falls in older adults and is seeking federal funding. Which plan is most appropriate?

options.text: Apply only to GAPNA, the main federal funder of aging research
options.rationale: GAPNA is a smaller, non-federal funding source.

options.text: Apply to Sigma Theta Tau, which is the largest federal agency
options.rationale: Sigma Theta Tau is a smaller, non-federal funding source.

options.text: Skip funding, since gerontologic research rarely shapes policy
options.rationale: Gerontologic nursing research has informed legislation and is integral to the Future of Nursing.

options.text: Look at NIA, HRSA, and grants.gov for federal funding options
options.rationale: Correct. Federal sources include NIA, HRSA, grants.gov, and the John A. Hartford Foundation.

questions.explanation: Gerontologic nursing research has grown since the early 1980s, has informed legislation, and guides practice and quality of life. Federal sources include NIA, HRSA, grants.gov, and the John A. Hartford Foundation; smaller sources include Sigma Theta Tau, ANF, and GAPNA.
